question: What is the main role of an epidemiological agent in disease?

options.A: Acting as a vital factor whose presence or absence causes illness
options.B: Increasing the overall immunity of the population
options.C: Determining the social status of patients
options.D: Serving as the physical environment where pathogens multiply

explanation: An epidemiological agent is the specific factor that must be present, or lack, for a disease to happen. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h1)

question: How are nutritional deficiencies different from biological pathogens?

options.A: Nutritional deficiencies only affect young children
options.B: Nutritional deficiencies mean a vital element is missing, while pathogens are living organisms
options.D: Nutritional problems cannot be managed at primary health care centers

explanation: Epidemiological agents include both harmful living entities like pathogens and the lack of necessary elements like proper nutrients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h1)

question: Which type of agent causes malaria?
explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which are single-celled protozoan parasites. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h2)

question: A patient comes in with Lassa fever. What kind of agent causes this?
explanation: Lassa fever is a viral illness spread through contact with items or food contaminated by rodent urine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h2)

question: Why is having too much or too little of a dietary component considered an epidemiological agent?

options.A: Because food always contains active pathogens
options.B: Because abnormal nutrient levels directly cause deficiency or lifestyle diseases
options.C: Because food items act as living carriers of disease
options.D: Because diet changes the temperature of the community

explanation: Agents in epidemiology are not just living organisms; nutritional elements whose excess or lack causes disease also count. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h3)

question: Which of the following is classified as a physical agent of disease?
explanation: Radiation, physical forces, and extreme temperatures are physical agents that can cause tissue damage. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h3)

question: What does the infectivity of an agent measure?

options.A: The proportion of infected people who show severe symptoms
options.B: The speed at which a chemical destroys cells
options.C: The overall death rate in a population
options.D: The ability of the agent to enter, survive, and multiply within a host

explanation: Infectivity refers to how well a pathogen can establish an infection inside a susceptible host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h4)

question: An agent causes severe illness and high death rates in most people who catch it. What is this property called?
explanation: Virulence describes the severity of the disease produced by an infectious agent. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h4)

question: What is the main difference between a disease reservoir and a disease source?

options.A: A reservoir is found in hospitals, while a source is in rural areas
options.B: A reservoir causes chronic illnesses, whereas a source causes acute infections
options.C: A reservoir is an inanimate object, while a source is an animal
options.D: A reservoir is where the agent naturally lives and multiplies, while a source is what directly infects the host

explanation: The reservoir provides the natural home for survival, while the source is the immediate point of transmission to the host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h5)

question: Why are animal (zoonotic) reservoirs hard for public health nurses to control?

options.A: Animals show the same symptoms as humans and refuse medications
options.B: Wild animals move freely and cannot be easily isolated or vaccinated
options.C: Zoonotic agents only spread through direct contact with pets
options.D: Wild animal reservoirs only exist in remote forests outside health jurisdiction

explanation: Controlling animal reservoirs is tough because wild species roam widely and are difficult to monitor. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h5)

question: Which of these is an example of indirect transmission via a vector?

options.A: A patient touches a contaminated table with an open wound
options.B: A mother passes an infection to her baby during birth
options.C: An infected person coughs directly on a healthcare worker
options.D: A female Anopheles mosquito transmits malaria through a bite

explanation: Vectors like mosquitoes act as living carriers that transfer infectious agents to new hosts. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h6)

question: How does the epidemiological triangle help nurses stop disease outbreaks?

options.A: By predicting the exact end date of an epidemic
options.B: By proving that the environment causes all non-communicable diseases
options.C: By calculating the treatment cost for every patient
options.D: By identifying a point—agent, host, or environment—where an intervention can break the chain

explanation: Targeting any part of the triangle—weakening the agent, protecting the host, or changing the environment—stops the spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h6)

question: Which nursing action is an example of primary prevention against biological agents?

options.A: Treating severe complications in an intensive care unit
options.B: Conducting blood tests to detect malaria parasites
options.C: Administering routine childhood immunizations at a clinic
options.D: Providing physical therapy for stroke patients

explanation: Immunization prevents disease occurrence in healthy hosts, making it a primary prevention measure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h7)

question: Why is isolating an infectious patient an effective way to control an agent?

options.A: It changes the genetic makeup of the pathogen to make it harmless
options.B: It removes all environmental risk factors from the community instantly
options.C: It destroys the internal agent without using drugs
options.D: It stops the agent from leaving the patient to reach new, susceptible hosts

explanation: Isolation blocks the exit route, stopping transmission from an infected person to the wider community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T78#GNS214_U1_T78_h7)
